analysis.title: Compass Impulse: Datacentres: Powering the AI era (November 2026)
key_insights: Data centres are shifting from a niche real estate segment to a strategic infrastructure asset class at the intersection of digitalisation, power systems and national competitiveness. Investors using only a real-estate lens risk missing this.
Global data centre infrastructure investment rose from about USD 100 billion in 2015 to more than USD 500 billion in 2024. Some forecasts put annual investment above USD 1 trillion before 2030.

The current cycle is underwritten by large, well-capitalised hyperscalers with strong balance sheets, unlike earlier cycles that were limited by financing and fragmented demand. Governments are a second demand source through sovereign AI, semiconductor and domestic compute programmes.

Power, not capital, is the binding constraint on AI infrastructure. Grid capacity, electricity availability and permitting limit growth in Europe and North America, and transformer, switchgear and skilled labour shortages add friction.

Data centres use about 1.5% of global electricity, roughly Germany's annual generation, and the IEA expects about 3% by 2030. They already exceed 20% of electricity demand in Ireland and 25% in Virginia.
Grid connection lead times in several key markets run from multiple years to more than a decade. In CBRE's 2025 global survey, power availability displaced financing as the industry's top challenge.

Data centres are becoming energy assets. Operators are adopting flexible interconnection, behind-the-meter generation, battery storage and energy management. The IEA projects on-site gas and batteries could supply roughly one-third to almost half of incremental data centre power capacity by 2030.
On-site generation projects are concentrated in the US and mostly gas-fired. European grid operators are exploring how flexible data centre demand can support grid stability.

Data centre types carry different risk and return profiles: hyperscale, enterprise, edge and colocation. Stabilised colocation with diversified tenants offers infrastructure-like cash flows. Hyperscale and development-led strategies have more growth but higher capital intensity, tenant concentration and execution risk.

About 72% of European colocation capacity sits in the FLAP-D markets (Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris, Dublin). Growth is moving to second-ring markets (Brussels, Berlin, Marseille), the Nordics and Southern Europe (Madrid, Milan, Barcelona, Rome, Athens), where power is easier to get.

ENTSO-E data cited in the report show total European data centre electricity demand rising by more than 50% over 2025-2030 on average. Colocation is expected to grow about 30% a year versus 8% for hyperscale and enterprise.

Europe is more interventionist on regulation (Energy Efficiency Directive, permitting complexity, moratoria), and expansion in Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam and Paris is getting harder. The US is more decentralised and development-friendly, but local scrutiny is rising. Tighter European supply may support stronger pricing.
Rising US electricity demand is leading to more new gas-fired capacity, which may slow the renewable transition.

Overlooked risks: (1) thematic concentration across vehicles that all depend on compute demand, (2) climate exposure (Allianz: 79% of global capacity at elevated physical climate risk, 54% at chronic heat or drought stress), (3) transformer and switchgear constraints plus faster hardware obsolescence, (4) community opposition, (5) uneven AI monetisation, (6) credit market impact of AI debt funding.
In Q1 2026, at least 75 US data centre developments representing about USD 130 billion of capital were delayed or blocked, matching the cumulative total for all of 2025.
Per McKinsey (August 2026), only four in ten organisations report a positive bottom-line contribution from AI, and operating costs are cited as limiting wider deployment.

AI capex has been funded mainly by private markets and internal cash flow, and future spend will likely need much more debt. US tech investment-grade bond issuance rose 112.2% from 2024 to 2025 (USD 108.7bn to 230.6bn), against 10.4% globally.

Data centre correlation with traditional real estate is low: 0.58 with industrial, 0.37 with apartment and office, 0.20 with retail (FTSE-NAREIT monthly data, 2015-2025). They can diversify real asset portfolios while adding concentration to compute demand.

Top takeaways: power access is more valuable than land, inference may be the more durable demand driver, digital ecosystems deserve premiums, flexible power is strategic, European supply constraints support pricing, secondary power-rich markets gain share, and platforms controlling both compute and energy may hold durable advantages.

sector_views.rationale: Multiple reinforcing demand drivers (hyperscalers, AI, sovereign programmes) support structural growth, but power access, climate, community opposition and compute concentration shape returns.
Supply shortages, long connection queues and permitting challenges suggest continued pricing support for high-quality assets.
Stabilised colocation offers recurring, infrastructure-like cash flows and forms the backbone of Europe's digital infrastructure, with demand growth expected near 30% a year.

risk_factors: Thematic concentration: exposure across infrastructure, real estate and private equity is tied to the same driver, compute demand.
Climate: 79% of global data centre capacity is exposed to elevated physical climate risk, and heat, drought, flood or wildfire exposure can hurt risk-adjusted returns.
Electrical equipment constraints (transformers, switchgear, transmission) and faster AI hardware obsolescence can delay projects and raise capital needs.
Community opposition and moratoria: about 75 US projects worth roughly USD 130 billion were delayed or blocked in Q1 2026.
Uneven AI monetisation: only 39% of organisations report at least scaling AI, with operating costs limiting deployment.
Credit market contagion as AI capex shifts toward debt funding.
Reliance on new gas-fired generation may slow the renewable transition.
Hyperscale and development-led strategies carry construction, power, customer concentration and execution risk.
charts_described: Estimated AI capex by hyperscaler (AMD, Nvidia, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Apple, Oracle, Coreweave) 2024-2030e, with the axis up to about USD 1.4 trillion (Bloomberg, August 2026).

Chart of AI infrastructure, AI productivity and AI enabled revenues indexed to 12/2023 versus the S&P 500, with the report stating AI-driven infrastructure revenues outperformed broader equity benchmarks.
geopolitical: Governments in North America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia are launching sovereign AI, semiconductor and domestic compute strategies for technological sovereignty and national security.
European regulation (Energy Efficiency Directive, permitting limits, temporary moratoria) constrains capacity in established hubs.

tension_points.bull_case: Data centres combine contractual infrastructure-like cash flows with secular growth, and low correlation to traditional real estate (0.20 to 0.58) supports diversification within real asset portfolios.
tension_points.bear_case: Allocations across infrastructure, real estate and private equity may appear diversified but are all tied to compute demand, a single underlying driver.

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscaler spending shows no signs of fatigue, backed by strong balance sheets and cash flows, and AI infrastructure assets have outperformed the S&P 500.
tension_points.bear_case: Only four in ten organisations report a positive bottom-line contribution from AI, and future capex will need significantly more debt, raising credit contagion risk.

theme_stances.key_argument: Capital is no longer scarce and power is, so access to electricity and grid rights is the scarce asset for data centre investors.
theme_stances.evidence: capital is no longer scarce. Power is.

theme_stances.key_argument: Supply shortages, long connection queues and permitting challenges suggest continued pricing support for high-quality assets.
Future AI investment is likely to require significantly higher debt, which would affect credit markets and raise contagion risk.
theme_stances.evidence: Future investments are likely to require significantly higher debt.
